note:
The one emit-boundary rule this format still has: the SHORTEST SPELLING of a position (SPEC 4.1). No other tier reaches it — the accept tier encodes what it decoded, so every position it writes is already short.

Four shapes, and each decides something different. `[lon, lat, null]` loses its trailing null. `[lon, lat, ele, null]` loses only the trailing one, so a writer that dropped every null would fail here. `[lon, lat, null, time]` is UNCHANGED: dropping that null would move the time into the elevation channel, which is the whole reason the rule is about trailing channels and not about nulls. And a full-arity position with both channels present is written whole.

NO VALUE IN THIS CASE CHANGES. That is the assertion, not an absence of one. This format does not constrain a writer's precision (SPEC 4.1), so a writer that rounded `-3.6712345678901235` to six places would be CONFORMING and would still fail this case, because the tier compares what the writer produced against the document it was given. If your implementation rounds by choice, round somewhere the library's WRITE path does not reach.

This case carried the rounding rules until they left the format: ties to even at `340.25`/`340.75`, the scaled-multiplication trap at `0.15`, and a negative zero manufactured by rounding `-0.00000004`. `corpus/numbers/` held 48 reference roundings for the same rule. All of it went when SPEC 4.1 stopped requiring a writer to round, because a corpus that certifies a rule the format does not state certifies the wrong thing.
